source: Laukkonen, Ingledew, Grimmer, Schooler, Tangen (2022) Irrelevant insights make worldviews ring true (Scientific Reports)
finding: Preregistered demonstration and direct replication (same lab): an Aha on an anagram raises truth ratings of unrelated worldview statements. A 10-second delay between the anagram and the statement removes the effect.
numbers: Exp 1: two samples of 1500 recruited; 1250 and 1239 analysed. Aha vs no Aha truth rating 7.21 vs 6.35, d=.23 (demonstration) and 7.34 vs 6.52, d=.25 (replication). Anagram vs no anagram d=.46 and .29. Exp 2 (676 analysed): no-delay Aha effect d=.23; delay 6.20 vs 6.02, b=.12, p=.447; condition x Aha b=.70, p<.001.
limits: Same lab as the 2020 original. Effect size (d about .23-.25) is smaller than the 2020 d=.32 and .63. Aha rated after the truth judgment. About 17 percent excluded. Exp 2 sample accounting does not add up in the paper. Not an independent lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 8. The human spillover needs the claim and the Aha to be close in time. An agent analog is a stated-certainty shift right after a reframe inside one context. Not tested in LLMs. Cheap control: reset context between items.

source: Webb, Little, Cropper (2016) Insight Is Not in the Problem: Investigating Insight in Problem Solving across Task Types (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Largest human insight-monitoring dataset found (about 400 recruited over 3 experiments), but it uses post-solution feeling ratings, not warmth. Insight rating tracks correctness for insight problems and CRAs but hardly for non-insight problems. So no large warmth replication exists here.
numbers: Recruited 193 (Exp 1), 82 (Exp 1a), 129 (Exp 2); removed 9, 8, 12. Insight-accuracy correlation, insight problems / CRA / non-insight: Exp1 r=.50/.41/.02; Exp1a .40/.40/.24; Exp2 .495/.39/.19. Non-insight problems more accurate than classic insight problems (diff 11.02).
limits: No feeling-of-warmth measure. Final N per experiment not stated in the text read. Page read to 100000 of 114560 characters.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. Shows the label insight problem is weak and the solver report matters, which supports detecting impasse in code rather than trusting problem type or self-report.

source: Kumaran (2026) Reported Confidence in LLMs Tracks Commitment More Than Correctness
finding: Two-stage design: the model answers and gives confidence, later decides to commit or abstain. Verbal confidence predicts the commit decision better than correctness. Calibrated token log-probabilities do the reverse. Residual verbal confidence (after removing log-prob variance) is near chance for correctness.
numbers: Four non-reasoning models, SimpleQA and MMLU-Pro. Correctness AUROC: calibrated log-prob 0.62-0.80, verbal class 0.53-0.65, numeric verbal 0.51-0.68. Residual verbal confidence correctness AUROC mean 0.473 (Wilcoxon vs .5, p=.844); residual log-prob mean 0.686 (p=.0039). Abstention AUROC of residual verbal median 0.64 (range 0.54-0.77).
limits: Non-reasoning models, factual and multiple-choice questions, not insight items. Mechanistic part on Gemma 3 and 4 only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 1 (indirect). A separate later call is not itself a fix: later stated confidence mostly reflects commitment. Supports the guardrail: use log-prob or sample agreement, not self-report, and test AUROC for each.

source: Ghosh, Kumar, Garg (2026) Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
finding: Compares verbalized confidence, a hidden-state probe and sampling agreement. Verbal confidence is unstable across prompt templates and looks well calibrated only because it clusters near the base rate. Sampling agreement has about twice the resolution.
numbers: N=842 matched items, small Qwen models (0.5B-7.6B), PopQA, SimpleQA, GSM8K, MATH. Resolution: verbal 0.0316, probe 0.0515, behavioral consensus 0.0637 (2.02x verbal). ECE (15 bins): verbal 0.0366, probe 0.0500, consensus 0.0704. Brier: verbal 0.1713, probe 0.1524, consensus 0.1465. In 9 of 10 cells calibrated verbal confidence never exceeds 0.50. Two of five preregistered hypotheses falsified.
limits: Small open models, factual and math items, one lab. Consensus costs about 10x the inference of verbal confidence.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 7 (indirect). Ranking quality (resolution, AUROC) is the test, not ECE. Sample agreement is the stronger code-side signal but costs tokens.

source: Yang, Han, Pham, Kim (2026) The Mirage of Calibrated Confidence: Trajectory-Independence of Verbalized Confidence in Vision-Language Models
finding: Verbalized confidence barely responds to what the reasoning trajectory contains. Masking trajectory tokens does not lower confidence monotonically; confidence rises at complete masking. Calibration training can worsen the disconnect while ECE looks fine (example ECE=0.081).
numbers: Hesitation test: share of items where confidence changes by less than .02 after cutting the model's own hesitation is 78.5 percent for Qwen3-VL (one model quoted). TGS-Bench over 10 benchmarks.
limits: Vision-language models, not insight items. Only the first model's 78.5 percent was read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. A model can say Wait, recheck and still report high confidence: trajectory-blind. Supports reading the trace in code, not the stated confidence.

source: Sourav, Balwani (2026) The Tell-Tale Trace: Detecting Reasoning Failures in LLMs Using Chain-of-Thought Dynamics
finding: On Boolean satisfiability, failed traces show repetition and low transition entropy; early warning works for some models only near the end of the trace. On UNSAT items models wrongly claim SAT by checking candidate assignments (wrong procedure, not wrong answer).
numbers: Dynamics-only features, UNSAT diagnosis AUROC 0.800 (Llama3-8B), 0.795 (Llama3-70B), 0.905 (OLMo2-13B) on the full trace; sentences before the answer only: 0.507, 0.570, 0.569. Llama3-70B false SAT claims 0.800 of UNSAT completions; accuracy 0.526 SAT vs 0.159 UNSAT. Proof-search prompt raises Llama3-70B from 13.3 to 85 percent (oracle-assisted, post hoc).
limits: Synthetic SAT, Llama/OLMo/Qwen3 open models. Threshold set without false-alarm cost. Intervention oracle-selected and unmatched in length to the generic retry. Authors say repetition is the robust signature; length and verification effects depend on model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Repetition and low transition entropy are code-readable stuck signals, but pre-answer AUROC is near chance (0.51-0.57) on UNSAT. A repeated-candidate detector works late, not early.

source: Grunefeld, Hojer, Mondorf, Plank, Rogers, Hardmeier, Heinrich, Frellsen (2026) Tracing Uncertainty in Language Model Reasoning
finding: Shape features of the token-uncertainty curve (slope, linearity) predict final correctness; correct traces show a steeper and less linear decline in uncertainty. The first 300 tokens already give AUROC 0.80 on GSM8K.
numbers: Five models, GSM8K and ProntoQA, 5-fold CV. Logistic regression AUROC on GSM8K: Llama 3.1 0.783, Llama 3.2 0.758, Qwen 2.5 0.807, DeepSeek R1 0.786, Qwen 3 0.727. Self-Certainty baseline 0.491-0.728. ProntoQA is weaker for several models (Qwen 2.5 0.519, Llama 3.2 0.550). CRV prior art 0.702 vs 0.783.
limits: Math and logic, not insight. Trained classifier per model on labeled data.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Uncertainty slope is a useful code-side signal but AUROC (0.5-0.8) is model and task dependent, so it needs per-model calibration before gating a reframe.

source: Chen, Cheng, Han, Keselj (2026) I May Not Have Articulated Myself Clearly: Diagnosing Dynamic Instability in LLM Reasoning at Inference Time
finding: A token-probability instability score (step-to-step distribution shift plus entropy) predicts wrong answers with above-chance AUC, weaker in the first 50 steps, near random on some small models.
numbers: GSM8K (first 300 test items): AUC(wrong) about 0.66 (greedy) to 0.74 (stochastic); first-50-step window 0.605; one model near random (about 0.52). Other tasks AUC 0.57-0.78.
limits: Small Llama models, math QA; no insight items.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Modest early AUC means an impasse gate will have many false alarms; reconsideration must be cheap.

source: Song, Li, Liu (2026) Prefix-Safe Bayesian Belief Tracking for LLM Reasoning Reliability: Separating Calibration from Ranking
finding: Prefix-time reliability estimates: scalar scores (entropy, verifier confidence) improve Brier but not AUROC; AUROC gains need structure-aware evidence and only when strong length-aware baselines have not absorbed it.
numbers: Open-weight traces on MATH-500, GSM8K, AIME 2025, RIMO-N. Best structure-aware observations +0.110 AUROC over standard prefix-safe baselines in the strongest hard-math setting.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; tables not checked. Math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Length-aware baselines are strong; any new impasse detector must beat trace length as the null baseline.

source: Song, Oh, Lee, Jo, Jo (2026) ThinkBrake: Efficient Reasoning via Log-Probability Margin Guided Decoding (v5)
finding: Reasoning models often reach a correct intermediate answer, keep going and overwrite it with a wrong one. Oracle stopping at the best sentence boundary raises accuracy; a training-free log-prob margin gate for the think-close token keeps accuracy and cuts tokens.
numbers: Oracle stop at each sentence boundary: average accuracy +8 percent with 72 percent fewer thinking tokens (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, BFCL). ThinkBrake: token reduction up to 30 percent (abstract); one table row 79.7 average accuracy with -26.5 percent tokens.
limits: Math and tool use, not insight riddles. The oracle number is hindsight, not achievable. Practical accuracy gain is small.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 outside Japanese riddles: the correct candidate appears and is lost. Recovery needs a commit rule keyed to a candidate seen in the trace; the oracle gap bounds the gain.

source: Caldarella, Talon, Aljundi, Ricci, Mancini (2026) Thinking Past the Answer: Evaluating Harmful Overthinking in Large Reasoning Models
finding: Defines the first correct prefix. Stopping there beats default reasoning; further reasoning often drops an already-correct answer. Plain early stopping cuts verbose overthinking but not harmful overthinking. Free-form answers show more harm than multiple choice.
numbers: Stop at first correct prefix beats default by nearly 10 percent on average, up to 21 percent in one setting. Harmful overthinking rate .11 multiple choice vs .24 free-form. Early stopping raises the harmful rate from 10.1 (no stop) to 18.4 (K=5) and 14.1 (K=2). Early stopping cuts verbose overthinking up to 50 percent.
limits: Mostly multimodal math benchmarks with a language-only check. Oracle stop uses the answer key.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6. A fixed early stop is not a commit rule. Forced candidate check needs a verifier to avoid locking in a lure. Free-form items are riskier than choices.

source: Hosseini, Nawathe, Salmani, Razaviyayn, Feizi (2026) Early Stopping for Large Reasoning Models via Confidence Dynamics (CoDE-Stop)
finding: Correct trajectories reach high-confidence intermediate answers early; wrong ones run long with unreliable confidence. A confidence-dynamics stop cuts tokens with similar accuracy to full reasoning.
numbers: Token use down 25-50 percent vs full-length reasoning. Table: vanilla 68.70 / 94.10 / 94.80 / 55.20 percent accuracy on four benchmarks; CoDE-Stop (Wait variant) 67.80 / 92.40 / 94.50 / 52.50 with fewer tokens.
limits: Math and science benchmarks. Compared with other early-stopping methods, not with self-consistency voting at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. Gates reduce tokens; this paper gives no evidence that a gate beats sample-and-vote at equal tokens on insight items.

source: Jindal, Akuthota, Taneja, Sharma (2026) The Path of Least Resistance: Guiding LLM Reasoning Trajectories with Prefix Consensus (PoLR)
finding: Clustering short prefixes of sampled traces and expanding only the dominant cluster matches or beats self-consistency at lower cost. Early prefix agreement predicts correctness.
numbers: Matches or exceeds SC on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, GPQA-Diamond; token use down up to 60 percent, latency down up to 50 percent.
limits: Math and science QA. Compared with SC, not with entropy-gated reconsideration; no insight items.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. The equal-token baseline for any impasse gate is cheap sample-and-vote with prefix filtering, not plain SC.

source: Fascendini, McGregor, Gupta, Griffiths (2026) The Riddle Riddle: Testing Flexible Reasoning in Large Language Models and Humans
finding: Riddle-like questions with a literal answer act as lures. Nine frontier LLMs fall for the riddle form; humans fail the opposite way.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 30 matched riddle sets, 100 humans (573 trials). LLM accuracy genuine riddles 84.9 percent vs riddle riddles 50.7 percent; humans 50.5 vs 80.5 (permissive coding; strict human 36.7 vs 77.4). 90.8 percent of LLM errors on riddle riddles were inappropriate inventive reasoning; 57.6 percent of human errors on genuine riddles were over-literal. Memorisation: a more memorised riddle OR 1.43 better on the genuine riddle, OR 0.76 worse on its matched riddle riddle. LLM judge vs human coder kappa .90-.93.
limits: Does not measure confidence or Aha. LLM-as-judge coding. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 6. Closest LLM analog of a false insight: committing to the clever reading. No verifier arm was tested, so the effect of a verifier is still open.

source: Kim, Luo, Kim, Lee, Li, Yang (2026) Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty
finding: Standard LLMs correct themselves mostly after an overt error (reactive); reasoning models also doubt without any error (proactive), but most of that doubt is unneeded. A minimal doubt cue injected into failed traces recovers some.
numbers: Precision of proactive corrections on reasoning models averages 24.4 percent (about three of four are on traces that were fine). Injecting a minimal doubt cue recovers about 15 percent of incorrect rollouts (Qwen3-8B/14B-Base; AIME24, AMC23, MATH500, 8 rollouts per problem); recovery falls as the truncation point moves later, near zero at 0.9 with no cue. Suppressing epistemic tokens lowers accuracy about 10 percent in one figure. 800 SFT samples can instill or suppress the habit.
limits: Math benchmarks; base models for the injection test; every rollout is wrong by construction.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 10. Model-chosen doubt is noisy; a code-injected doubt cue is cheap and works on failed traces. Fits the S6 design (code decides, not the model).

source: Rahmani, Krishna, Wang, Naghiaei, Yilmaz (2025) Self-Correcting Large Language Models: Generation vs. Multiple Choice
finding: Self-correction behaves differently by format: open generation improves fast in the first iterations and then risks semantic drift; multiple choice improves steadily but is capped by the options.
numbers: Six models; DisambiguationQA and other tasks. Generation improves in the first one or two iterations, then answers flip; multiple choice gains more gradually. Exact accuracy deltas not extracted.
limits: Not insight items; abstract, introduction and a results scan read.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, partial. Supports splitting open versus choice items when judging whether a reframe helps.

source: Ismayilzada, Cuomao, Yurshevich, Sotnikova, van der Plas, Bosselut (2026) CresOWLve: Benchmarking Creative Problem-Solving Over Real-World Knowledge
finding: 2,061 real-world creative puzzles. Models do worse on creative than factual questions (up to a 17 percent drop). They often retrieve the right facts but fail to connect them. Thinking models beat non-thinking.
numbers: 2,061 examples, five difficulty levels. Creative minus factual gap up to 17 percent. Reasoning effort raises accuracy, for example 9.4 to 17.8 percent (English) and 15.4 to 26.9 percent (Russian) from no thinking to medium effort for one model.
limits: No monitoring or confidence measure in what was read. Which model gave the 9.4/17.8 numbers was not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Failing to connect known facts matches an unnoticed impasse; supports a candidate-check step but is no direct test.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do LLMs Signal When They're Right? Evidence from Neuron Agreement Decoding
finding: Activation sparsity and cross-sample neuron agreement identify correct candidates within the first 32 tokens, matching majority voting on math and science and beating Avg@64 on open coding where voting is not usable.
numbers: Token use cut by 99 percent with minimal quality loss (abstract). Correct responses activate fewer unique neurons than incorrect ones.
limits: Needs white-box activations. Math, science, coding; no insight items. Abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9. Sets an internal-signal ceiling, but is not available for API-only agents.

source: Token-level verification mirage (2026) protocol sensitivity of entropy verifiers (ICML 2026 listing, snippet only)
finding: Search snippet only: under controlled within-problem evaluation on hard math, entropy-based verifiers that look like 0.80+ AUROC in looser settings fall to about 0.60-0.75; with a fixed scoring direction, final-token entropy is about 0.47-0.48.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite the numbers without opening.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Warning that entropy AUROC can be inflated by per-problem direction choice.

source: Gap search log (this session): queries for LLM warmth, entropy gate vs voting, verifier on FIAT-type items, large warmth replication

The web search quota ran out mid-session, so absence is not proof.
